channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: France's 10-year yield is just under 5% and its spread over German Bunds rose above 150 basis points in the week before Handelsblatt's 9 October report, for the first time since the euro debt crisis.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that high debt, rising bond yields and political blockades are making France a risk factor for the eurozone; the 10-year yield, just under 5%, reached the highs of the 2008 financial crisis. The government is trying to pass its last budget before the 2027 presidential election without its own majority. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's push for an austerity budget for 2027, aimed at cutting tens of billions of euros in spending, has sparked student protests, Cnyes reports, and former ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet called on French parties to save themselves first; activation of rescue tools such as the ECB's TPI and the ESM depends on France taking the initiative. The reporting does not give the exact spread or yield on a dated close, the budget deficit target, or ratings agencies' positions.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The spread is a market measure of risk for France relative to Germany, and the budget outcome is still open. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, higher sovereign yields raise borrowing costs for companies in the same country and can tighten financing for construction and investment. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, France is a large European market for construction, automotive and consumer goods, so a tighter budget and higher rates could weigh on demand there. Points that may be worth considering include the budget vote, any rating action, and whether the spread moves to other eurozone countries.

Handelsblatt | Cnyes

item.title: President Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine on 11 October, but Putin has so far rebuffed proposals for an energy ceasefire, Zelenskyy said he was not aware of it, and Russian strikes hit Ukrainian power plants afterwards.
item.description:
Trump said on 11 October that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop strikes on each other's energy infrastructure, effective immediately, but gave no details, Arab News reports. LiveMint reports that Putin has so far rebuffed proposals for an energy ceasefire and that Trump announced a similar ceasefire on 14 September, after which both sides continued their strikes. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said the ceasefire was news to him and that Ukraine would accept one if Russia did, The Guardian reports. Zelenskyy said power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on 11 October, causing power outages in Kyiv, CNA reports. According to Commercial Times, Trump had previously demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries, blaming these attacks for higher diesel prices. The reporting does not give any terms or monitoring arrangement, or a Russian response to this specific announcement.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Putin has so far rebuffed such proposals and strikes followed the announcement, so it is a claim rather than an agreed arrangement. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, attacks on Russian refineries have reduced Russian product exports, so a working halt on energy targets would add refined-product supply to world markets, while continued strikes keep that supply uncertain. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the effect would run through diesel and other refined-product prices into logistics and some solvent costs. Points that may be worth considering include a Russian response to this announcement and whether strikes on refineries stop.

Arab News | LiveMint | The Guardian | CNA | Commercial Times

item.title: China's National Development and Reform Commission has issued a 2026–30 circular-economy plan that calls for green product design and more recycled materials, targeting about a 16% rise in major resource productivity by 2030.
item.description:
The plan sets targets and measures across production, consumption, recycling and resource use for the 15th Five-Year Plan period, China Daily reports. It calls for wider adoption of green product design, greater use of recycled materials, more orderly trading of second-hand goods and improved recycling networks. By 2030 it aims to raise major resource productivity by about 16% from 2025 levels and targets annual use of major renewable resources at 510 million metric tons, with output of the resource-recycling industry expected to reach CNY 8 trillion. The reporting does not name product categories, standards or recycled-content quotas, does not say whether packaging is covered by specific measures, and does not describe enforcement. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The plan sets national targets and directions, but the reporting gives no product rules, so its effect depends on the standards that follow. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, green product design rules typically address how products can be repaired, taken apart and recycled, which reaches the materials used to join components. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, design-for-recycling requirements can favour bonding solutions that separate cleanly or are compatible with recycling streams. Points that may be worth considering include the implementing standards for product design and recycled content, and which product groups they name first.

China Daily

item.title: Hurricane Isaias shut in 62.89% of US Gulf of Mexico oil production and 57.35% of gas production, with undamaged facilities expected to restart after safety checks.
item.description:
Around 1.28 million barrels a day of oil and 1.13 billion cubic feet a day of gas were shut in, and personnel were evacuated from 121 production platforms, Anadolu Agency reports, citing the Marine Minerals Administration. Production at undamaged installations is expected to resume immediately after standard safety checks, while damaged facilities may need more time. The port of Mobile, Alabama, suspended all operations ahead of the storm, MarketScreener reports. Isaias made landfall on the night of 9 October near Destin, in northwest Florida, as a Category 2 hurricane, weakened over Alabama and became a post-tropical cyclone, La Nación reports; more than 850,000 customers lost power. LiveMint reports that the storm arrived while the cost of moving US crude to Asia was already high. The reporting does not say how long the shut-ins lasted, whether any platforms or refineries were damaged, or whether Gulf Coast petrochemical plants stopped.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The shut-ins were large, and the source expects undamaged sites to resume immediately after standard safety checks, but the reporting does not say how long the interruption lasted. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the US Gulf Coast also hosts a large share of US refining and petrochemical capacity, so a storm can affect product supply even when offshore output returns. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, several resins, solvents and monomers come from Gulf Coast plants, so outages at any of them could matter. Points that may be worth considering include reports of damage at offshore or onshore facilities, the restart timeline, and any force majeure notices from chemical producers in the region.

Anadolu Agency | MarketScreener | La Nación | LiveMint

item.title: China's industry ministry has proposed stricter rules on car design and R&D testing, including a ban on fully hidden door handles and reliability tests of at least 30,000 km, with comments open until 10 November.
item.description:
The industry ministry drafted the rules with three other agencies because some manufacturers had rushed out new models without enough validation, raising safety and environmental risks, MarketScreener reports. The draft bans fully hidden door handles, foldable or flexible displays and the use of "zero-gravity" or swivel seats while driving, and key functions such as lights and wipers must keep physical controls. From 1 January 2027, automakers seeking approval for new models must submit more technical details on innovative designs and testing; models that are poorly tested or backed by false data will be rejected; models already approved must file information by 1 July 2027. Beijing Daily reports requirements for reliability verification of no less than 30,000 kilometres and an environmental adaptability cycle of at least one year, and that industry experts see the rules curbing the trend of ever-shorter development cycles. The reporting does not say how many current models would be affected or whether imported vehicles are covered.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rules are a draft open for comment, so details may change before they apply. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, longer and documented validation periods slow the pace at which new models and design features reach the market. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, materials in new vehicle designs are qualified within these testing cycles, so longer validation can lengthen qualification time for new bonding and sealing solutions in China while making approved specifications more stable. Points that may be worth considering include the final text after 10 November and whether testing requirements apply to components and materials as well as complete vehicles.

MarketScreener | Beijing Daily

item.title: Daily charter rates for very large crude carriers from the Persian Gulf to East Asia rose 40% in the week to 8 October to over USD 1.4 million, a record and around 14 times the pre-war level, Commercial Times reports.
item.description:
The rate was around USD 100,000 a day before the US–Iran war at the end of February, passed USD 1 million for the first time on 14 September and kept setting records, Commercial Times reports; in the first week of October, up to the 8th, it rose 40% from the previous week. Of around 850 such tankers in service, over 40% are concentrated in or heading to the Persian Gulf, according to Signal Ocean data. The report attributes the tight supply of ships to the war hampering tanker scheduling, and says Gulf producers such as Saudi Arabia have to carry out inefficient ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman because the Strait of Hormuz is blocked by warfare. Separately, hiring a very large crude carrier to move US oil to Asia now costs around USD 79 million, according to the Baltic Exchange, which LiveMint puts at roughly USD 39.50 a barrel for a 2-million-barrel cargo. The reporting does not give rates for product tankers or chemical tankers, or for routes to Europe.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures are daily charter rates and voyage costs for very large crude carriers on specific routes, so they measure the cost of moving crude rather than the price of crude itself. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, when freight becomes a large part of a cargo's value, buyers favour nearer supplies and long-haul trade becomes less economic, which can change regional price differences. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, higher crude freight reaches feedstock costs through refiners' margins and can widen price gaps between regions. Points that may be worth considering include whether rates for product and chemical tankers follow, and whether the share of tankers tied up in the Gulf falls.

Commercial Times | LiveMint

item.title: European carmakers cut investment by 20% in 2026 while large European companies in other sectors raised theirs by 10%, an Allianz Trade study finds, with value added per car sold in Europe down 30–45% since 2021/22.
item.description:
Economists at Allianz Trade, the credit insurance subsidiary of the Allianz group, say Europe's carmakers spent their capital for too long on dividends, short-term returns and combustion-engine technology instead of investing early in digitalisation and electrification, Handelsblatt and Süddeutsche Zeitung report. According to the study, value added per car sold in Europe has declined by between 30% and 45% since 2021/22, and carmakers reduced investment by 20% in 2026 although the technological gap to Chinese competitors in batteries and digitalisation threatens to widen. Frankfurter Rundschau reports from the same study that the market shares of Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes-Benz have fallen by around ten percentage points in Europe and seven in China since 2021. The reporting does not give the absolute investment amounts, whether the 20% covers carmakers only or suppliers too, or the regional split of the cuts.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The study is an assessment by economists, with its own figures for investment and value added. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, lower carmaker investment slows new model programmes and plant retooling, which is where new material specifications are usually set. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, structural bonding, battery assembly and lightweighting solutions enter vehicles through new platforms, so reduced investment can delay qualification of new applications in Europe while Chinese competitors keep their pace. Points that may be worth considering include whether carmakers' 2027 capital plans confirm the cut, how suppliers' investment moves, and whether share losses continue.

Handelsblatt | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Frankfurter Rundschau

item.title: The EU says China will limit hybrid and plug-in hybrid exports to the EU to half or less of the level the EU projects over four years, under a deal that, according to the EU, also facilitates access to rare earths.
item.description:
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič announced the agreement on 9 October after two days of talks in Beijing, MarketScreener reports; Šefčovič said the deal could cut imports by several million cars over four years. The FT reports that the commitment would still allow actual volumes to increase, that China did not immediately confirm the details, and that a joint statement refers to an "understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles in a manner consistent with [World Trade Organization] rules". Šefčovič said the deal also facilitates access to rare earths, Euronews reports. Lianhe Zaobao reports EU officials as saying China would reduce tariffs on EU goods by EUR 225 million; China's Ministry of Commerce, as reported by China Daily, says the two sides agreed to explore the possibility of reducing tariffs on certain goods. According to China's Ministry of Commerce, as reported by China Daily, the EU will advance procedures for company-specific price undertakings in its electric-vehicle anti-subsidy case. EU leaders are to review the outcome at their summit in Brussels the following week, with the EU's trade deficit with China at more than EUR 1 billion a day. A day earlier, 44 European industry associations, including chemicals, had urged faster trade defence. The reporting does not give the projected base, an annual limit, how compliance is monitored, or the goods covered by the tariff cuts.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The hybrid limit rests on the EU's account and is set against a projection rather than current volumes, so, on the EU's account, it limits growth while still allowing actual volumes to increase. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a negotiated export limit can ease pressure for broader trade defence, while EU leaders may still judge it insufficient. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the balance between imported and European-built vehicles affects where automotive bonding and sealing demand sits, and access to rare earths matters for electric motors in vehicles and machinery. Points that may be worth considering include whether China confirms the volumes, how EU leaders judge the deal at the summit, and whether access to rare earths improves in practice.

MarketScreener | The Financial Times | Euronews | Lianhe Zaobao | China Daily | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: The Rhine at Cologne stands at 40 cm, a historic low, after months of drought that have forced inland shipping companies and businesses along the river to look for alternatives, Tagesschau reports.
item.description:
Inland navigation, ferry operations and the economy along the Rhine have been affected by drought for months, Tagesschau reports. The water level at Cologne is currently 40 centimetres, a historic low; at Duisburg the river reached its lowest point in September at 1.22 metres. The report describes the Rhine as one of the most important trade routes for the region and says that, because of the record low level, inland skippers, shipping companies and businesses have had to look for alternatives for months to keep shipping running. In Cologne's Rheinauhafen nothing has been moving for some time, and most sports boats moored there stayed in the harbour all season. The reporting does not give load limits for barges, freight surcharges, the volume of cargo shifted to rail or road, or effects on named industrial sites along the river, and it does not give a forecast for the water level. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The report measures a water level and describes months of disruption, but gives no freight or volume data, so the cost of the low water is not quantified. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, low water on the Rhine reduces how much a barge can carry, which raises freight costs per tonne and moves cargo to rail and road with limited spare capacity. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, chemical sites and raw-material flows in western Germany depend partly on Rhine shipping, so a prolonged low level can raise inbound costs and lengthen delivery times. Points that may be worth considering include how long the low level lasts, whether freight surcharges are reported, and whether chemical producers along the river report restrictions.

Tagesschau

item.title: China's passenger vehicle sales fell 24.6% year on year in September to about 1.69 million units, on a high 2025 base, but rose 9.7% from August, China Daily reports, citing the China Passenger Car Association.
item.description:
China Daily reports, based on China Passenger Car Association information, that the year-on-year decline was due to a high comparison base in 2025. The same report gives company figures for September: BYD sold 463,561 new energy vehicles, up 17% from September 2025, and exported 179,877 passenger cars and pickups, up 153.9%; Geely sold 292,168 vehicles and exported 106,700, up 162%; Chery sold 292,308 vehicles, with total sales up 4.2% year on year and record exports of 207,814; SAIC sold around 406,000 vehicles, with overseas shipments of 150,000, up 49.1%. The reporting does not split the national total into domestic sales and exports, does not say what made the 2025 base high, and does not give the year-to-date total or a forecast for the rest of the year. It rests on one source. The company figures are not all on the same basis: BYD's is new energy vehicles, the others are total vehicles.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The national decline is year on year against a base the source calls high, while the month-on-month figure and the company export figures point upward, so the source attributes the year-on-year fall to the comparison base, but does not say how underlying demand moved. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, strong export growth by Chinese carmakers means more Chinese-built vehicles compete in other markets, while domestic volume sets demand for parts made in China. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly uses structural bonding, sealing and battery materials, so the split between Chinese domestic sales and exports affects where that demand is supplied from. Points that may be worth considering include the export share in the national total, how the October figures compare, and how export growth meets EU limits on hybrids.

China Daily

item.title: The US Treasury has authorised transactions in Russian diesel until 7 April 2027, after a Trump–Putin deal under which, Trump announced, Russia is to release 300,000 tonnes immediately, 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1 million tonnes.
item.description:
The authorisation, announced minutes after a call between Presidents Trump and Putin, covers the sale, delivery, offloading and importation, including into the US, of Russian-origin diesel until 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 7 April 2027, Business Standard reports. The FT reports that Trump announced the volumes as 300,000 tonnes "immediately", 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes "immediately thereafter", that the Kremlin confirmed the deal, and that wholesale diesel for delivery in New York harbour fell about 4.5% to USD 4.67 a gallon after the announcement. Russia partially lifted its ban on diesel exports with immediate effect, The Economic Times reports. Analysts cited by The Guardian forecast little "meaningful" effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas; according to calculations using US Energy Information Administration figures, the 300,000 tonnes equate to about three-quarters of one day's US use. Germany's Fuels und Energie association says the EU's import ban on Russian diesel, in place since 5 February 2023, remains and, given the volumes reportedly agreed, expects no significant effect on the world market and prices or major effects at German petrol stations. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the move gives Russia revenues to wage war. The reporting does not say who pays for the diesel, which buyers outside the US will take it, or how prices moved beyond the New York reaction.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The decision allows Russian diesel volumes announced by Trump to reach the US and world markets while the EU keeps its import ban. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, its effect on Europe would run through world product prices rather than through direct supply; diesel prices feed into freight and distribution costs, and a small addition to a tight market can still move refined-product spreads. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, transport is part of the delivered cost of raw materials and finished goods, so a lower diesel price would ease logistics costs while leaving feedstock costs to crude and gas. Points that may be worth considering include whether the November volume arrives on time, how European diesel prices respond with the EU ban unchanged, and whether the authorisation is extended or withdrawn.

Business Standard | The Financial Times | The Economic Times | The Guardian | Handelsblatt | New Indian Express

item.title: At the Critical Chemicals Alliance assembly on 8 October, the Commission announced short-term action for the chemical sector, including a list of around ten critical chemical molecules by the end of the year and stronger trade measures.
item.description:
The second General Assembly of the Critical Chemicals Alliance took place on 8 October in Creutzwald, on the Franco-German border, with industry, trade unions and policymakers, IndustriAll Europe reports. Commission Executive Vice-President Stéphane Séjourné reaffirmed the Commission's commitment to strengthening the sector. He announced further action in the short term: a targeted list of around ten critical chemical molecules by the end of the year, enhanced trade monitoring and stronger trade measures, together with an investment agenda to be negotiated under the next Multiannual Financial Framework. IndustriAll describes the meeting as taking place at a critical moment for Europe's chemical industrial base. The reporting does not name the molecules or the criteria for selecting them, what support or protection a listed molecule would receive, which trade instruments are meant by "stronger trade measures", or the size of the investment agenda. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The announcement sets a date for a list but leaves its content and consequences open, so it marks the direction of EU chemicals policy rather than a measure in force. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, a short list of critical molecules would single out a few upstream chemicals for priority treatment, and trade measures on those molecules could change import prices and availability for downstream users. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, many formulations rely on base chemicals and intermediates made in Europe and imported, so the choice of molecules could affect whether the policy supports supply security, raises input costs, or both. Points that may be worth considering include which molecules reach the list, whether trade measures attach to them, and how the investment agenda is funded in the next budget.

IndustriAll Europe
